questions.title: Cutting a Losing Position Against Your Own Hope
questions.prompt: You're holding a position that has moved against you well past the point where your own pre-trade thesis said you'd exit, but you still believe the thesis is right and the market just hasn't caught up yet. Walk through how you'd handle the decision to cut it.
questions.modelAnswer: The discipline here is to treat the pre-committed exit rule as binding specifically because it was set before I had an emotional or sunk-cost stake in being right about this particular trade. I'd cut the position at the predetermined level, not because I necessarily believe the thesis is wrong, but because 'I still believe I'm right, the market just hasn't caught up' is exactly the rationalization every losing position generates, and a risk process that only holds when it agrees with your current conviction isn't actually a risk process. If I genuinely still believe in the underlying thesis after exiting, that's a separate decision to re-enter with a fresh, appropriately sized position and a new, explicit risk plan -- not a reason to hold through a level I already decided, with a clearer head, that I wouldn't tolerate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd cut it at the level I set before I had a stake in defending this specific trade, full stop. 'The market hasn't caught up yet' is the exact sentence every losing position eventually produces, so I don't trust it as a reason to override a rule I set with a clearer head. If I still believe in the thesis afterward, that's a fresh decision to re-enter with new sizing and a new plan -- it's not a justification for holding through a level I already decided I wouldn't.
commonMistakes: Treating conviction in the thesis as a valid override for a pre-committed exit rule
Not recognizing 'the market hasn't caught up yet' as a common rationalization pattern rather than new information
Conflating 'exit this position' with 'abandon this thesis forever' rather than treating re-entry as a separate decision
keyPoints: Pre-committed exit rules exist precisely to be binding when conviction and emotion are pulling the other way
Continued belief in a thesis is not a valid reason to override a predetermined risk level
Exiting and re-entering with a fresh plan are two separate, legitimate decisions
Rationalizing a held losing position is a predictable pattern, not special insight

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly commits to honoring the pre-set exit rule
Recognizes the rationalization pattern at play
Separates the exit decision from the broader thesis/re-entry decision
Professional, composed framing of the answer

questions.title: Communicating a Drawdown to Risk Management
questions.prompt: Your strategy is down 60% of its monthly loss limit, 10 days into the month. Risk management asks you for an update. Walk through what you'd actually tell them.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd lead with the concrete numbers, not a narrative: current P&L, percent of the monthly limit used, and how that compares to what the strategy's historical volatility would predict for this point in the month -- is this within a normal range of variation, or is it already outside what the backtest or recent live history would lead us to expect. Then I'd state plainly what I've already checked: whether this looks like normal, expected variance versus a sign something about the strategy's risk profile has changed, referencing whatever monitoring data supports that read (realized vs. expected volatility, any specific trades or days driving the drawdown). I'd close with a clear statement of what I'm doing about it right now -- continuing to run within limits and watching closely, proactively reducing size, or flagging for a deeper review -- rather than leaving risk management to infer my plan. The goal is to give them an accurate, complete picture quickly, not to minimize the number or oversell confidence that everything is fine.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give them the numbers first -- where P&L stands, what fraction of the limit that represents, and whether that's within the normal range of variation for this strategy at this point in a month or something that already looks unusual. Then I'd tell them plainly what I've checked so far to figure out which of those it is, and close with exactly what I'm doing about it right now, not leave them to guess my plan. What I wouldn't do is downplay the number or oversell confidence I don't actually have that it's fine.
commonMistakes: Leading with reassurance or a narrative rather than the concrete numbers
Not contextualizing the drawdown against the strategy's expected/historical variance
Failing to state a clear current action plan, leaving risk management to ask follow-up questions
keyPoints: Lead with concrete numbers: current P&L, percent of limit used, comparison to expected variance
State what's already been checked to distinguish normal variance from a real problem
Close with a clear, specific statement of current action, not just a status update
Avoid minimizing the situation or overselling confidence that isn't warranted yet

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with concrete, specific numbers
Contextualizes the drawdown against expected variance
States a clear current action plan
Professional tone, free of minimization or overselling

questions.title: Handling a Big Winning Month Without Overconfidence
questions.prompt: You just had your best month ever, well above what your strategy's historical Sharpe ratio would predict as typical. How do you talk about this result with your desk, and what do you watch out for in your own thinking?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd present the result honestly as an outlier relative to the strategy's historical distribution of returns, not as evidence the strategy's true edge has suddenly improved -- a single standout month is exactly the kind of outcome a normal, if favorable, draw from a volatile return distribution would occasionally produce, and treating it as proof of a stronger edge is the same statistical mistake as panicking over one bad month. The thing to actively watch for in my own thinking is the temptation to increase size based on this one result, since that's sizing off a lucky realization rather than off the underlying edge estimate, which hasn't actually changed just because one month went unusually well. I'd keep running the position sizing the same process-driven way I would have before the good month, and if anything use the result as a reminder to double-check that the strategy's risk controls would have handled an equally large move in the other direction just as well.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be straightforward that this is an outlier relative to what the strategy's history says to expect, not proof the edge suddenly got bigger -- a great month is a normal, if lucky, draw from the return distribution, the same way a bad month usually is. The thing I'd actively guard against is sizing up because of it; that's reacting to a lucky outcome rather than to any real change in the underlying edge. If anything, I'd use a result like this as a prompt to check that the risk controls would have handled an equally large move the other way just as well.
commonMistakes: Treating an outlier good month as evidence the strategy's true edge has improved
Increasing position size in response to a lucky result rather than a change in the underlying edge estimate
Presenting the result to the desk with more confidence than the statistics actually support
keyPoints: A single standout month is a plausible outlier draw, not proof of an improved edge
Sizing up in response to a lucky result is a common and costly overconfidence mistake
Continue the same process-driven sizing approach regardless of one favorable outcome
Use the result as a prompt to re-verify risk controls symmetrically, not just celebrate it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the result as a statistical outlier, not proof of improved edge
Explicitly identifies the temptation to size up as a risk to avoid
Professional, measured communication framing
Demonstrates genuine self-awareness rather than performative humility

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Senior Trader on Sizing a Position
questions.prompt: A senior trader on your desk wants to size a new position at roughly double what your own risk analysis suggests is prudent given the strategy's estimated edge and its uncertainty. How do you raise your disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise it directly and specifically, grounded in the actual numbers rather than a vague feeling of discomfort: walk through my sizing estimate, state explicitly what assumption or input it's most sensitive to (for example, how much the sizing changes if the edge estimate's confidence interval is wider than assumed), and ask what input or view the senior trader is using that leads to a different, larger number. The goal is a genuine comparison of assumptions, not a status contest -- if their reasoning reveals information or a view I hadn't fully weighted, I should be willing to update; if mine reveals an estimation-uncertainty risk they hadn't fully weighted, they should be willing to reconsider. I'd also make clear this is specifically about position size relative to estimated edge and its uncertainty, not a disagreement about whether the trade itself is a good idea, since conflating those two makes the conversation unnecessarily adversarial.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through my own numbers directly -- here's my sizing estimate, here's what it's most sensitive to -- and ask what's driving theirs to come out so much higher. I'm not trying to win an argument, I'm trying to find out whether they have information I'm missing or whether I have an estimation-uncertainty concern they haven't fully weighted. And I'd keep it specifically about sizing, not the trade itself, because folding those two questions together just makes it a harder, more personal conversation than it needs to be.
commonMistakes: Raising the disagreement vaguely ('I'm not comfortable with this') rather than with specific numbers and assumptions
Treating the conversation as a status contest rather than a genuine comparison of reasoning
Conflating disagreement about position size with disagreement about whether the trade itself is worth doing
keyPoints: Ground the disagreement in specific numbers and the assumptions driving them
Frame it as comparing reasoning, not winning an argument or deferring purely to seniority
Be genuinely willing to update if the senior trader's reasoning reveals something you missed
Keep the disagreement specifically about sizing, separate from the underlying trade thesis

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Grounds the disagreement in specific, concrete reasoning
Frames the conversation collaboratively rather than adversarially
Shows genuine openness to updating based on the senior trader's input
Professional communication and composure

questions.title: Explaining a Backtest's Limitations Honestly to a Skeptical Risk Manager
questions.prompt: A risk manager pushes back hard on your backtest's results, pointing out that you tried many parameter variations before landing on the one you're presenting. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd acknowledge the concern directly rather than getting defensive, because it's a legitimate and well-founded one: testing many parameter variations and keeping only the best-performing one is exactly the multiple-testing / data-dredging problem that can make a pure-noise strategy look great by chance alone. I'd walk through specifically what I did to guard against it -- how many variations were actually tried, whether I used a deflated Sharpe ratio or similar adjustment that discounts the result for the number of trials, and whether the final choice was validated out-of-sample on data that wasn't used during the search at all. If I can't fully answer those questions, I'd say so honestly rather than overstating my confidence, and treat the risk manager's skepticism as a legitimate prompt to go back and do that validation properly before asking for capital, rather than as an obstacle to argue past.
questions.professionalAnswer: That's a fair challenge, not an attack -- trying lots of variations and keeping the best one is exactly the setup that makes noise look like skill. I'd walk through what I actually did about it: how many variations were tested, whether the result holds up after adjusting for that with something like a deflated Sharpe ratio, and whether it was validated on data the search never touched. If I can't answer those cleanly, I'd say so and go do that work properly rather than argue the risk manager into accepting a result I can't fully defend.
commonMistakes: Getting defensive rather than treating the pushback as a legitimate, well-founded concern
Not being able to specify concretely how many variations were tested or how overfitting risk was addressed
Overstating confidence in the result rather than honestly acknowledging gaps in the validation
keyPoints: Multiple-testing / data-dredging is a real and well-documented risk when many variations are tried
A credible response specifies what was actually done to guard against it (deflated Sharpe, out-of-sample validation)
Honesty about gaps in validation is more professional and more credible than overstated confidence
Treat the risk manager's skepticism as a legitimate prompt to strengthen the work, not an obstacle

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges the multiple-testing concern as legitimate rather than defending reflexively
Describes concrete safeguards (deflated Sharpe, out-of-sample validation)
Demonstrates honesty about any remaining gaps
Professional, non-defensive tone

questions.title: Owning a Fat-Finger Error
questions.prompt: You submitted an order with the wrong size due to a manual entry mistake, and it created an unwanted position that lost money before you caught it. Your supervisor asks you to explain what happened. How do you handle this conversation?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd state plainly and specifically what happened -- the exact mistake (wrong size entered), when I caught it, what I did immediately after catching it (closed the position, how quickly), and the resulting P&L impact -- without minimizing it or burying the key facts in a longer explanation of context. I'd avoid blaming the system, the market, or anyone else for what was a manual entry error on my part, since an honest, specific account is both the right thing to do and the only way the firm can actually learn from the incident. I'd then proactively propose a concrete safeguard that would have caught this before it happened -- a confirmation step on large or unusual order sizes, for instance -- rather than waiting to be asked, since taking ownership includes contributing to the fix, not just the apology.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it simple and factual: here's exactly what happened, here's when I caught it, here's what I did immediately after, here's the P&L impact. No blaming the system or the market for what was a manual mistake on my end. And I'd come in with a proposed fix already in mind -- a confirmation step for unusual order sizes, for example -- rather than waiting to be asked what should change, because owning it means being part of the fix, not just the apology.
commonMistakes: Minimizing the error or burying the key facts in excessive context
Deflecting blame onto the system, the market, or someone else
Only apologizing without proactively proposing a concrete safeguard
keyPoints: Give a plain, specific, factual account of what happened and when
Take direct ownership without deflecting blame
State the concrete impact (P&L, timing) honestly
Proactively propose a safeguard to prevent recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a clear, specific, factual account
Takes direct ownership without deflection
Proactively proposes a concrete preventive safeguard
Professional composure throughout

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Trader Who Wants to Size Up a Hot Streak
questions.prompt: A junior trader you mentor has had three good weeks in a row and wants to double their position size, convinced their edge has gotten bigger. What do you tell them?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd walk them through the actual math rather than just telling them no: three good weeks is a small sample, well within the range of normal variance a genuinely unchanged edge would produce some of the time, and the Kelly framework they should already know says position size should track the estimated edge and its uncertainty, not a recent, short-run result. I'd specifically ask what evidence, beyond the recent P&L itself, suggests the underlying edge has actually changed -- a structural change in the market, a genuine improvement in their process -- versus what's simply a good run. If there's no such evidence, sizing up now is sizing off noise, not signal, and I'd point out that the Kelly framework's own warning about estimation error applies just as much to a recent hot streak updating your belief about mu as it does to an initial backtest estimate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the math with them rather than just saying no: three good weeks is a small sample that a genuinely unchanged edge would produce some of the time just by variance. I'd ask directly what's actually changed about their process or the market, versus what's just a good run -- if there's no real answer to that, sizing up now is sizing off noise, which is exactly the estimation-error trap Kelly sizing warns against, just showing up as excitement about a hot streak instead of overconfidence in a backtest.
commonMistakes: Simply forbidding the size increase without explaining the underlying reasoning
Not connecting the situation back to the Kelly/sizing framework the junior trader should already know
Failing to ask what concrete evidence, beyond recent P&L, would actually justify believing the edge changed
keyPoints: A short winning streak is a small, noisy sample that doesn't by itself indicate a changed edge
Position sizing should track the estimated edge and its uncertainty, not a recent short-run result
Ask for concrete evidence of a real change versus a lucky run
This is the same estimation-error risk the Kelly framework warns about, applied to a hot streak rather than a backtest

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the statistical reasoning rather than just issuing a directive
Connects the situation to the Kelly/estimation-error framework
Asks for concrete evidence distinguishing a real change from noise
Demonstrates genuine mentoring tone, not just a correction

questions.title: Flagging Your Own Strategy for a Retirement Review
questions.prompt: You've been running a strategy for two years and genuinely enjoy trading it, but your own rolling-Sharpe monitoring has flagged it for a retirement review per the pre-committed rule. Nobody else has noticed yet. What do you do?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise it myself, proactively, rather than waiting for someone else to notice -- the entire point of setting a pre-committed monitoring rule was to remove exactly this kind of in-the-moment temptation to look the other way because I'm personally attached to the strategy. I'd bring the actual rolling-Sharpe data to whoever owns the review process, present it plainly, and let the pre-agreed process run its course rather than making a private case for why this time is different. If the review concludes the strategy should be resized or retired, I'd treat that as the system working as intended, not as a personal loss, and if there's a genuine argument that this instance is different from the rule's typical case, that argument belongs in the review discussion with the data on the table, not in a decision to quietly keep running it unflagged.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag it myself and bring the data to the review process, because the whole reason that pre-committed rule exists is to take this exact decision out of my hands when I'm the one most attached to the outcome. If I think this case is genuinely different, that argument belongs in the review with the numbers on the table, not in a private decision to just keep running it quietly because nobody else noticed yet.
commonMistakes: Waiting for someone else to notice rather than proactively raising the flag
Treating personal attachment to the strategy as a valid reason to quietly bypass the pre-committed rule
Making a private case for an exception instead of bringing the argument to the actual review process
keyPoints: Pre-committed monitoring rules exist specifically to remove personal bias from this decision
Proactively surface the flag rather than waiting for someone else to catch it
Any argument for an exception belongs in the formal review, with the data, not in a private decision
Treat the outcome of the review as the system working correctly, not a personal failure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Commits to proactively raising the flag rather than staying silent
Correctly explains the purpose of a pre-committed rule in removing personal bias
Demonstrates integrity and professional maturity in handling the personal attachment
Clear, direct communication

questions.title: Evaluating a Trading Offer Beyond the Headline Number
questions.prompt: You have two competing offers: one at a prop trading firm with a lower base and a profit-share tied heavily to your own individual trading, and one at a bank quant desk with a steadier base and bonus less tied to individual P&L. How do you think through the decision?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start by recognizing these two offers have genuinely different compensation structures, not just different numbers -- the prop firm's profit-share-heavy structure can pay far more in a good year and far less in a bad one than the bank desk's steadier, less individually-linked structure, so comparing a single headline total-compensation figure between them without accounting for that variance is comparing apples to oranges. I'd build a researched range for each, specific to firm type and city, from aggregated salary data, direct market postings, and my own network, rather than trusting one borrowed number for either. Beyond compensation, I'd weigh strategy and risk culture fit (does the prop firm's approach to risk match how I actually want to trade), mentorship and learning curve (will I be taught or left to figure it out alone), and my own honest tolerance for the prop firm's higher variance -- a profit-share structure that's lucrative in good years and thin in bad ones suits some people's risk tolerance and financial situation far better than others', and that's a genuinely personal factor, not something either offer letter will tell me.
questions.professionalAnswer: These aren't really comparable on a single number -- one's profit-share-heavy with real upside and real downside tied to my own trading, the other's steadier and less individually linked. I'd build a researched range for each rather than trusting either headline figure alone, and then weigh risk-culture fit, mentorship, and my own honest tolerance for the prop firm's variance, since that's a personal factor neither offer letter is going to tell me about. The 'right' answer genuinely depends on which of those tradeoffs fits me, not on which number looks bigger on paper.
commonMistakes: Comparing the two offers purely on a single total-compensation number without accounting for structural variance differences
Not researching an independent, firm-type-specific range rather than trusting one borrowed figure
Ignoring risk-culture fit, mentorship, and personal variance tolerance as real decision factors
keyPoints: Prop and bank-desk compensation structures carry genuinely different risk/variance profiles, not just different numbers
Build an independently researched compensation range specific to firm type and city for each offer
Weigh strategy/risk-culture fit and mentorship alongside compensation
Personal tolerance for compensation variance is a legitimate, individual factor in the decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the structural difference in compensation variance between the two offers
Proposes building an independently researched range rather than trusting a single number
Weighs non-compensation factors (risk culture, mentorship)
Demonstrates mature, personal-fit-based reasoning rather than a purely numeric comparison

questions.title: Staying Disciplined in the First Minutes of a Volatile Open
questions.prompt: The market opens sharply against several of your positions on unexpected overnight news, and everyone on the desk is reacting fast and loudly. How do you keep your own decision-making disciplined in those first few minutes?
questions.modelAnswer: The first few minutes of a volatile, news-driven open are exactly when pre-committed rules matter most, precisely because they're the moments least suited to fresh, careful judgment -- prices are moving fast, information is incomplete, and everyone around me reacting loudly adds social pressure to do something immediately. I'd check my positions against pre-set risk limits and let any kill-switch-level breaches do what they're designed to do automatically, rather than second-guessing or overriding them in the moment. For positions still within limits, I'd resist the urge to make a major directional decision based on the first few minutes of noisy, fast-moving price action, and instead give myself a brief, deliberate pause to actually understand what the news is and how it specifically affects each position's real exposure, rather than reacting to the market's reaction. Reacting fast is not the same as reacting well, and the desk being loud is not itself new information about what the right move is.
questions.professionalAnswer: That first stretch is exactly when I trust the pre-set rules rather than my own judgment in the moment -- any hard limit breaches, I let the kill switch do its job rather than second-guessing it live. For everything still within limits, I give myself a deliberate pause to actually understand what the news means for each specific position, rather than reacting to how fast prices are moving or how loud the desk is. Reacting fast and reacting well aren't the same thing, and nobody else's volume in the room is new information about what I should actually do.
commonMistakes: Overriding or second-guessing a kill-switch breach in the heat of the moment
Making a major decision based purely on the speed/noise of price action rather than understanding the actual news
Treating the desk's collective urgency as itself a signal about the correct response
keyPoints: Pre-committed rules matter most exactly when conditions are least suited to careful fresh judgment
Let kill-switch-level breaches act automatically rather than second-guessing them in the moment
Take a deliberate pause to understand the actual news before reacting to price action alone
Social pressure/urgency from others on the desk is not itself information about the right move

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Commits to trusting pre-set rules/kill switches rather than overriding them under pressure
Describes a deliberate pause to understand the actual situation before reacting
Explicitly separates social pressure from actual decision-relevant information
Professional, composed framing
